intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene on chromosome 19.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is caused by homozygous mutation in the CCDC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Therefore, CCDC9 may be a novel pathogenic gene associated with severe asthenozoospermia.
checks.explanation: The paper presents CCDC9 only tentatively, as a candidate gene in a single patient. It does not use the SPGF104 designation or state causation firmly.

checks.claim: The CCDC9 gene is located on chromosome 19.
checks.explanation: NC_000019.9 is the chromosome 19 reference sequence, so the location follows from the variant notation.

paragraphs.text: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility characterized by severe asthenozoospermia, in which fewer than 1% of spermatozoa in the ejaculate are motile, with severely damaged sperm morphology and ultrastructure (Sha et al., 2019).

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-104 (SPGF104) is a form of male infertility characterized by severe asthenozoospermia.
checks.evidence_quote: severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat to the male reproductive health
checks.explanation: The phenotype is severe asthenozoospermia. SPGF104 is standard OMIM nomenclature for it.

checks.claim: In SPGF104, fewer than 1% of spermatozoa in the ejaculate are motile.
checks.evidence_quote: Owing to less than 1% of motile spermatozoa in the ejaculated semen, severe asthenozoospermia is a serious threat
checks.explanation: The abstract states this figure directly.

checks.claim: In SPGF104, sperm morphology and ultrastructure are severely damaged.
checks.evidence_quote: its morphology and ultrastructure were severely damaged in the spermatozoa containing the novel variant
checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

paragraphs.text: Sha et al. (2019) studied a man with severe asthenozoospermia from a consanguineous family. The morphology and ultrastructure of his spermatozoa were severely damaged.

checks.evidence_quote: we identified a novel homozygous variant in CCDC9 (NC_000019.9: g.47763960C>T, NM_015603.3, NP_056418.1: p. Ser109Leu) in a patient from a consanguineous family
checks.explanation: The patient has severe asthenozoospermia, which is a male phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Khan et al. (2025) recruited 7 large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, 5 of which had a history of consanguinity. In 1 of these families, a genetic cause in CCDC9 was identified.

checks.evidence_quote: We recruited seven large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, including five with a history of consanguinity.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.evidence_quote: We recruited seven large families with clinically diagnosed male infertility from rural Pakistan, including five with a history of consanguinity.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Khan et al. (2025) identified a genetic cause in CCDC9 in 1 of the 7 Pakistani male infertility families.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified plausible genetic causes in five of the seven families, including a homozygous 10 kb deletion of exon 2 in a well-established male infertility gene (M1AP), and biallelic missense substitutions (SPAG6, CCDC9, TUBA3C)
checks.explanation: Five solved families matched to five genes, so CCDC9 accounts for one family.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SPGF104 in the family reported by Sha et al. (2019) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance: the affected man, from a consanguineous family, was homozygous for a CCDC9 mutation. Khan et al. (2025) likewise identified biallelic CCDC9 missense variants in a Pakistani family with male infertility.

paragraphs.text: In a man from a consanguineous family with severe asthenozoospermia, Sha et al. (2019) identified a homozygous missense mutation in the CCDC9 gene (g.47763960C-T, NC_000019.9), resulting in a ser109-to-leu (S109L) substitution. In silico analysis predicted the variant to be highly pathogenic. CCDC9 protein levels were significantly low in the patient's spermatozoa.

agent.process_note: I read both papers in full, but only abstracts were available for each. Sha et al. (2019) gives the CCDC9 S109L variant, with genomic and protein notation but no c. notation. Khan et al. (2025) reports biallelic CCDC9 missense variants in one Pakistani family but does not name the variants, give the family's consanguinity status or describe the patients' phenotype, so I did not invent any of these. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so I wrote no gene MIM number; I inferred the chromosome-19 location from the NC_000019.9 accession in Sha et al. I found no data on segregation, sperm parameters beyond motility, or the specific ultrastructural defects.
